title: Ice Growth and Decay in a Tibetan Plateau Reservoir: The Coupled Controls From Local Meteorology and Under‐Ice Processes
content:
Abstract

Most reservoirs on the Tibetan Plateau experience seasonal ice cover, yet the mechanisms of their ice processes remain poorly understood. This study monitored ice growth and decay at a typical reservoir over two consecutive winters (2023–2025). Continuous surface heat loss, driven by the Plateau's cold and windy climate with prevailing clear skies, led to average ice growth rates of 1.0 and 0.8 cm day−1 before melting with maximum ice thicknesses of 33.1 and 22.0 cm. Average basal melt rates were 3.1 and 1.8 cm day−1 during the melting periods, exceeding the surface melt rate (1 cm day−1), due to strong solar radiation and snow-free ice surface. Net longwave radiation dominated the surface heat loss and ice growth, followed by the turbulent heat flux under the region's clear-sky, low-humidity, and windy conditions. The water-ice heat flux F w regulated the basal heat budget and exhibited pronounced seasonal and interannual variations, decreasing during ice growth due to declined transmitted radiation and water temperature, further reduced during snow-covered periods, but rising sharply during melting. Water-level drawdown likely suppressed F w through under-ice heat loss, while warm inflows enhanced F w , accelerating melting. The mean F w were 41.9 and 30.6 W m−2 respectively for these two ice-seasons, took up 37% and 40% of the conductive heat flux during growth, and were entirely used for basal ablation during melting. These findings provide deep insight into the seasonal evolution of ice cover in Tibetan Plateau reservoirs and highlight the impacts of reservoir operation and unique highland climate.
